body:
Malony, a 33-year-old psychiatric nurse, was diagnosed as having low levels of adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH). The deficiency of this hormone will result in...

a. the reduced secretion of cortisol
b. the increased secretion of estradiol
c. the increased secretion of aldosterone
d. increased secretion of sex hormone binding globulin
e. pigmentation of her palms due to elevated levels of MSH

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. the reduced secretion of cortisol | **T** | ACTH drives cortisol secretion. |
| b. the increased secretion of estradiol | **F** | Not caused by ACTH deficiency. |
| c. the increased secretion of aldosterone | **F** | Aldosterone is mainly controlled by renin–angiotensin and K⁺; it is largely preserved, not increased. |
| d. increased secretion of sex hormone binding globulin | **F** | Not a consequence. |
| e. pigmentation of her palms due to elevated levels of MSH | **F** | Pigmentation occurs in primary adrenal failure with high ACTH/POMC, not ACTH deficiency. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Secondary adrenal insufficiency** (low ACTH) reduces **cortisol** (and adrenal androgens), but **aldosterone** is largely maintained by the renin–angiotensin system, so hyperkalaemia is uncommon. **Hyperpigmentation** is absent because POMC-derived peptides (ACTH, MSH) are low – in contrast to Addison's disease.

## Simplified explanation

Low ACTH → low cortisol, no pigmentation, aldosterone roughly normal.

body:
The biochemical features of Addison's disease include...

a. ↑ K⁺ and ↑ H⁺
b. decreased GFR
c. decreased urine sodium
d. ↓ Na⁺ and ↓ aldosterone
e. depletional hypernatraemia

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. ↑ K⁺ and ↑ H⁺ | **T** | Aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalaemia and mild acidosis. |
| b. decreased GFR | **T** | Volume depletion reduces GFR (pre-renal uraemia). |
| c. decreased urine sodium | **F** | Urinary sodium is inappropriately high (salt wasting). |
| d. ↓ Na⁺ and ↓ aldosterone | **T** | Hyponatraemia with low aldosterone. |
| e. depletional hypernatraemia | **F** | Depletional hyponatraemia. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **primary adrenal failure (Addison's)** deficiency of **aldosterone and cortisol** causes **renal sodium wasting** (high urine Na), **hyponatraemia**, **hyperkalaemia**, mild **metabolic acidosis**, volume depletion with **reduced GFR/raised urea**, hypoglycaemia; ACTH is high (pigmentation).

## Simplified explanation

Addison's: low sodium, high potassium and acid, low GFR, salty urine.

body:
Consider the following statements about acromegaly.

a. Hyperphosphataemia is a common occurrence
b. Insulin-like growth factor 1 is reduced in acromegaly
c. The patient with acromegaly will be overtly diabetic
d. Growth hormone excess can also lead to prolactinoma
e. Diagnosis can be confirmed by the glucose tolerance test

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Hyperphosphataemia is a common occurrence | **T** | GH increases renal tubular phosphate reabsorption. |
| b. Insulin-like growth factor 1 is reduced in acromegaly | **F** | IGF-1 is raised (screening test). |
| c. The patient with acromegaly will be overtly diabetic | **F** | Impaired glucose tolerance is common; overt diabetes in a minority. |
| d. Growth hormone excess can also lead to prolactinoma | **F** | Some adenomas co-secrete prolactin, but GH excess does not cause prolactinoma. |
| e. Diagnosis can be confirmed by the glucose tolerance test | **T** | Failure of GH to suppress during an OGTT confirms acromegaly. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acromegaly: screen with **IGF-1 (raised)**; confirm by **failure of GH suppression** (< 1 µg/L) during a 75 g **OGTT**. GH is anti-insulin – IGT is common, overt diabetes in ~20–30%. **Hyperphosphataemia** and hypercalciuria occur.

## Simplified explanation

Acromegaly: high IGF-1, GH not suppressed by glucose, often high phosphate.

body:
Madam P, a 47-year-old woman, was diagnosed with panhypopituitarism after several months of being unwell. The following statement(s) is/are correct about her condition.

a. She could have primary hypothyroidism
b. All her trophic hormone levels will be normal
c. All her trophic hormone levels will be reduced
d. She will have hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism
e. The TRH and CRH tests will be enough to diagnose her condition

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. She could have primary hypothyroidism | **F** | Her hypothyroidism is secondary (low TSH). |
| b. All her trophic hormone levels will be normal | **F** | They are reduced. |
| c. All her trophic hormone levels will be reduced | **T** | Panhypopituitarism = deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones. |
| d. She will have hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism | **T** | Low FSH/LH → gonadal failure. |
| e. The TRH and CRH tests will be enough to diagnose her condition | **F** | All axes must be assessed (combined pituitary function tests, GH, gonadotrophins, prolactin). |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c T, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Panhypopituitarism** is loss of all anterior pituitary trophic hormones (GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH/LH, prolactin), causing **secondary** hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and **hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism**. Assessment uses basal hormones plus dynamic tests of each axis (e.g. insulin tolerance, synacthen, GnRH, TRH).

## Simplified explanation

All pituitary hormones are low, giving secondary thyroid, adrenal and gonadal failure.

body:
A 54-year-old tanker driver complained of headaches, visual problems and frequent urination. He was diagnosed with posterior pituitary damage due to a pituitary adenoma. The man's condition will be diagnosed with...

a. Serum renin
b. Urine osmolality
c. VMA estimation
d. Serum aldosterone
e. Water deprivation test

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Serum renin | **F** | Not used for DI. |
| b. Urine osmolality | **T** | Inappropriately dilute urine. |
| c. VMA estimation | **F** | For phaeochromocytoma. |
| d. Serum aldosterone | **F** | Not used for DI. |
| e. Water deprivation test | **T** | The definitive test for diabetes insipidus. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b T, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Posterior pituitary damage causes **cranial diabetes insipidus** (ADH deficiency): polyuria with dilute urine. Diagnosis uses paired **plasma and urine osmolality** and the **water deprivation test** (urine fails to concentrate), followed by **desmopressin** (urine then concentrates in cranial DI).

## Simplified explanation

Diabetes insipidus is diagnosed with urine osmolality and the water deprivation test.

body:
Unless clinically indicated, thyroid function tests should not be performed until patients have recovered from non-thyroidal illnesses (NTI) because .....in NTI.

a. Plasma [TSH] is occasionally increased
b. Plasma [TSH] is occasionally decreased
c. Plasma [free T3] is occasionally increased
d. Plasma [total T3] is occasionally increased
e. Plasma [total T3] is often decreased

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Plasma [TSH] is occasionally increased | **T** | Transiently, especially during recovery. |
| b. Plasma [TSH] is occasionally decreased | **T** | In acute illness and with dopamine/steroids. |
| c. Plasma [free T3] is occasionally increased | **F** | Free T3 is typically low (reduced T4→T3 conversion). |
| d. Plasma [total T3] is occasionally increased | **F** | It falls. |
| e. Plasma [total T3] is often decreased | **T** | 'Low T3 syndrome'. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid syndrome)**, reduced peripheral **5'-deiodinase** activity lowers **T3** (and raises reverse T3); in severe illness T4 also falls. **TSH** may be **low** in the acute phase and transiently **high** during recovery. Results can mimic thyroid disease, so testing is deferred.

## Simplified explanation

Illness lowers T3 and makes TSH swing up or down, so wait until recovery.

body:
In the third trimester of normal pregnancy:

a. Plasma [total T3] is often increased
b. Plasma [free T4] is often reduced
c. Plasma alkaline phosphatase activity is often increased
d. Plasma urea is often increased
e. Plasma albumin is often decreased

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Plasma [total T3] is often increased | **T** | Raised TBG increases total hormones. |
| b. Plasma [free T4] is often reduced | **T** | Free T4 falls slightly in late pregnancy. |
| c. Plasma alkaline phosphatase activity is often increased | **T** | Placental ALP. |
| d. Plasma urea is often increased | **F** | GFR rises, so urea falls. |
| e. Plasma albumin is often decreased | **T** | Haemodilution. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c T, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Pregnancy: oestrogen raises **TBG** (total T4/T3 rise), free T4 tends to fall in later pregnancy; **placental ALP** rises; **GFR increases ~50%**, lowering urea and creatinine; plasma volume expansion lowers **albumin**.

## Simplified explanation

In late pregnancy total T3 and ALP rise; urea and albumin fall; free T4 dips a little.

body:
Women taking oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives are likely to have increased plasma concentration of:

a. Albumin
b. LDL cholesterol
c. Fasting triglycerides
d. Cortisol
e. Copper

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Albumin | **F** | Albumin tends to fall slightly. |
| b. LDL cholesterol | **F** | Oestrogen tends to lower LDL. |
| c. Fasting triglycerides | **T** | Oestrogen increases hepatic VLDL production. |
| d. Cortisol | **T** | Raised cortisol-binding globulin increases total cortisol. |
| e. Copper | **T** | Raised caeruloplasmin. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c T, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Oestrogens increase hepatic synthesis of **binding proteins** (CBG, TBG, SHBG, **caeruloplasmin**, transferrin), so **total cortisol**, total T4 and **copper** rise; they raise **triglycerides** and HDL and lower LDL.

## Simplified explanation

The pill raises binding proteins (so total cortisol and copper go up) and triglycerides.

body: What is the clinical significance of the following tests? i. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies ii. Metyrapone test iii. 21-day progesterone test iv. Cortisol:creatinine ratio v. Pregnancy-associated plasma protein (PAPP-A) *(10 marks)*
answer:
i. **Anti-TPO antibodies** – markers of **autoimmune thyroid disease** (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease); predict progression of subclinical to overt hypothyroidism and postpartum thyroiditis.

ii. **Metyrapone test** – metyrapone blocks **11β-hydroxylase**, lowering cortisol; a normal pituitary responds with a rise in ACTH and **11-deoxycortisol**. Used to assess **ACTH (pituitary) reserve** in suspected secondary adrenal insufficiency and to help differentiate Cushing's disease (responds) from adrenal/ectopic causes.

iii. **Day-21 (mid-luteal) progesterone** – confirms **ovulation** in a 28-day cycle (≥ ~30 nmol/L indicates ovulation); used in infertility work-up.

iv. **Urine cortisol:creatinine ratio** – a convenient screening test for **Cushing's syndrome** (hypercortisolism) on a spot/early-morning urine, correcting for urine concentration.

v. **PAPP-A** – a placental protein measured in the **first-trimester combined screening** for **Down's syndrome** (low PAPP-A with high free β-hCG and increased nuchal translucency); low levels also predict adverse outcomes (growth restriction, pre-eclampsia).

> [!answer]
> Anti-TPO – autoimmune thyroid disease; metyrapone – ACTH reserve/Cushing's cause; day-21 progesterone – ovulation; cortisol:creatinine – Cushing's screen; PAPP-A – first-trimester Down's screening.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Endocrine tests are chosen to answer specific questions: is there autoimmunity, is the axis intact, is the woman ovulating, is there hypercortisolism, is the fetus at risk.

## Simplified explanation

Each test answers one question: thyroid autoimmunity, pituitary reserve, ovulation, Cushing's, Down's screening.

body: Briefly differentiate between the following: i. Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone ii. Cushing's disease and Cushing's syndrome iii. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism iv. 5α-reductase and aromatase v. Oestradiol and oestrogen *(10 marks)*
answer:
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| i | **Testosterone**: main androgen secreted by testicular Leydig cells; acts on Wolffian ducts, muscle, spermatogenesis | **Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**: more potent androgen formed from testosterone by 5α-reductase in target tissues; virilises external genitalia, prostate, hair follicles |
| ii | **Cushing's disease**: hypercortisolism due to an **ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma** | **Cushing's syndrome**: the clinical state of cortisol excess from **any cause** (pituitary, adrenal tumour, ectopic ACTH, exogenous steroids) |
| iii | **Hypogonadotrophic** (secondary) hypogonadism: **low FSH/LH** from hypothalamic/pituitary disease (e.g. Kallmann's, tumours) | **Hypergonadotrophic** (primary) hypogonadism: gonadal failure with **high FSH/LH** (e.g. Klinefelter's, Turner's, menopause, orchitis) |
| iv | **5α-reductase**: converts testosterone → DHT | **Aromatase**: converts androgens → oestrogens (testosterone → oestradiol, androstenedione → oestrone) |
| v | **Oestradiol (E2)**: the most potent specific oestrogen, mainly ovarian | **Oestrogen**: the general class of female sex steroids (oestradiol, oestrone, oestriol) |

> [!answer]
> DHT is the potent 5α-reduced form of testosterone; Cushing's disease is the pituitary cause of Cushing's syndrome; hypogonadotrophic = low LH/FSH, hypergonadotrophic = high LH/FSH; 5α-reductase makes DHT, aromatase makes oestrogens; oestradiol is one (the main) oestrogen.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Several of these pairs contrast a **specific** term with a **general** one (Cushing's disease vs syndrome; oestradiol vs oestrogen) or **opposite pathways** (5α-reduction vs aromatisation; central vs gonadal failure).

## Simplified explanation

DHT is stronger testosterone; Cushing's disease is one cause of the syndrome; low vs high FSH/LH; one enzyme makes DHT, the other oestrogen.

body: What reason(s) will you assign for the following occurrences? i. Hypothyroidism in women using hormonal contraceptives ii. Osteoporosis in post-menopausal women iii. Gynaecomastia in adult males iv. High TSH levels in prolactinoma v. Hirsutism *(10 marks)*
answer:
i. **Oestrogen raises TBG**, increasing total T4/T3 and binding; in women on thyroxine replacement, more T4 is bound so dose requirement rises – untreated they may appear hypothyroid; total hormone results also mislead if interpreted without free hormones.

ii. **Oestrogen deficiency** after menopause increases osteoclast activity (more RANKL, less osteoprotegerin) and bone resorption outpaces formation → loss of bone mass.

iii. **Increased oestrogen:androgen ratio** – increased aromatisation (obesity, ageing), liver cirrhosis, hypogonadism, oestrogen-secreting tumours, hCG tumours, drugs (spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine), hyperprolactinaemia.

iv. A large prolactinoma may compress the stalk, but **high TSH** usually reflects **primary hypothyroidism**: raised **TRH** stimulates both **TSH and prolactin** (and pituitary hyperplasia that can mimic prolactinoma).

v. **Androgen excess or increased follicle sensitivity**: PCOS, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumours, Cushing's syndrome, drugs (anabolic steroids); low SHBG raises free testosterone; idiopathic (increased 5α-reductase activity).

> [!answer]
> i. ↑TBG binding; ii. oestrogen loss → bone resorption; iii. high oestrogen:androgen ratio; iv. TRH from primary hypothyroidism stimulates TSH and prolactin; v. androgen excess (PCOS, CAH, tumours) or increased sensitivity.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Many endocrine findings reflect changes in **binding proteins**, the **balance** of sex steroids, or **shared hypothalamic drives** (TRH stimulates both TSH and prolactin).

## Simplified explanation

The pill raises binding protein; menopause removes oestrogen's bone protection; gynaecomastia is too much oestrogen vs androgen; TRH raises both TSH and prolactin; hirsutism is androgen excess.

body:
A 56-year-old shop-keeper who is mostly sedentary complained of fatigue, lethargy, attacks of giddiness and sweating. She also complained of irregular periods, which her doctor attributed to menopause and put her on oestrogen therapy. A fortnight later she collapsed and was taken to the Emergency Unit, where her plasma glucose was 2.3 mmol/L. Thyroid function: **fT4 4.1 (10–24)**; **TSH 0.78 (0.5–5.5)**; **fT3 2.8 (3.1–7.7)**.

i. Explain her results. ii. What is her diagnosis? iii. What is the cause of her low serum glucose concentration? iv. List three other tests and explain why they are useful in confirming the diagnosis. v. Comment on the pitfalls of using TSH as the primary screening test for hypothyroidism. *(10 marks)*
answer:
**i.** Low free T4 and low free T3 with an **inappropriately 'normal'/low TSH** – the pituitary is not responding to low thyroid hormones: **secondary (central) hypothyroidism**. Hypoglycaemia suggests additional **ACTH/cortisol (and GH) deficiency**.

**ii.** **Hypopituitarism** (e.g. pituitary tumour or Sheehan's syndrome) with secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency; irregular periods reflect **hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism** rather than true menopause.

**iii.** **Cortisol and GH deficiency** (counter-regulatory hormones) reduce gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; hypothyroidism adds to this – hence fasting hypoglycaemia.

**iv.** Any three:
- **9 am cortisol and ACTH / short Synacthen test** – confirm secondary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol with low/normal ACTH).
- **FSH, LH and oestradiol** – low gonadotrophins with low oestradiol confirm hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (a menopausal woman should have high FSH/LH).
- **Prolactin, IGF-1/GH** – other pituitary axes; prolactin may be high (stalk compression) or low.
- **Combined pituitary function test (insulin tolerance, TRH, GnRH)** and **pituitary MRI** – define reserve and cause.

**v.** TSH alone **misses secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism** (TSH normal or low), may be misleading in **non-thyroidal illness**, recovery phase, drugs (dopamine, glucocorticoids), early treatment of thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, TSH-secreting adenoma and assay interferences; free T4 should be measured when pituitary disease is suspected.

> [!answer]
> Low fT4/fT3 with inappropriately normal TSH = secondary hypothyroidism; diagnosis hypopituitarism (with ACTH/GH deficiency causing hypoglycaemia and gonadotrophin deficiency); confirm with cortisol/Synacthen, FSH/LH/oestradiol, prolactin/IGF-1 or pituitary tests; TSH-only screening misses central hypothyroidism.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **primary** hypothyroidism TSH rises; a low or 'normal' TSH with low free T4 indicates **pituitary/hypothalamic** failure, which usually involves other axes. Recognising coexistent **cortisol deficiency** is vital – thyroxine replacement before steroid replacement can precipitate adrenal crisis.

## Simplified explanation

Her thyroid hormones are low but TSH isn't high, so the pituitary has failed; low cortisol and GH explain the low sugar.
hint: TSH should be high if the thyroid were the problem.
